notes: \cpara{The image shows Captain Kirk and the Gorn, a reptilian alien played by stuntmen in costume, in the Star Trek episode ``Arena'' (1967).}
\cpara{Opens with satire: the aliens of film and television are humans in costume, in makeup, or in nothing at all.}
\cpara{Continues the irony: the human form as the universe's default.}
\cpara{Offers convergent evolution, ironically, as the explanation.}
\cpara{Turns Earth's own animals against that explanation: the longer ago a lineage split from ours, the less it resembles us.}
\cpara{Adds that real aliens might not use DNA or proteins at all.}
\cpara{Parodies arguments that intelligence requires a human body: two legs, upright walking, free hands.}
\cpara{Carries the parody on to eyes, noses, attractive females and English.}
\cpara{Gives the plain explanation as the punch line: costumed humans are the easy way out.}
\cpara{States the thesis: the real failure is aliens who think like humans, above all like English speakers of the author's own time.}
\cpara{An anecdote: the Americans of \textsc{Psycho} (1960) seemed to the author more alien than most screen aliens.}
\cpara{Says a writer must see their own culture as a special case. Suggests, with ``I suspect,'' that a year abroad would help more than reading history, and admits the author has not done it.}
\cpara{Says that seeing humanity itself as a special case is harder still.}

\cpara{The first sentence is hedged (``seem''); the second, that the six emotions are shown ``by the same facial expressions'' in every known culture, is not. That was a common claim, but it was disputed well before the post. Russell (\textsc{Psychological Bulletin}, 1994) argued that the supporting studies' methods may have shaped their results, and concluded that expressions and emotion labels ``are probably associated, but the association may vary with culture.'' A review by Barrett and colleagues (2019) found that how people show anger or fear ``varies substantially across cultures.''}

\cpara{Gives the reason humans are alike: in a sexual species, complex adaptations must be shared by everyone, or they would not assemble. The argument is set out in ``The Psychological Unity of Humankind'' (June 2008), which is not in the book.}

\cpara{States as fact that we evolved to predict other minds by putting ourselves in their place. In philosophy and psychology this is ``simulation theory,'' one side of a debate. Its rival, the ``theory-theory,'' holds that ``a tacit psychological theory underlies the ability to represent and reason about others' mental states'' (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, ``Folk Psychology as Mental Simulation''). The post does not mention the rival.}

\cpara{Answers the objection that we know others differ from us: brains are too complex to model except by running them on our own. The argument rules out modelling other brains ``neuron-by-neuron''; it does not consider an abstract model of goals and beliefs, which is what the rival view proposes. ``Belief in Intelligence,'' the previous post in the book, uses such a model to predict where a friend will drive.}
\cpara{Describes the method: you run a shadow of the other mind's anger and beliefs on your own brain, often without asking ``What would I do in this situation?''}
\cpara{Names the method ``empathic inference'' and says it works for humans, ``more or less.''}
\cpara{Says empathic inference fails for minds whose emotions differ from ours, as we cannot see as an alien from four-dimensional space would see.}
\cpara{Gives an example, an alien with no sense of humor, and a joke about an emotion we lack: ``you've never antled.''}

\cpara{Anticipates the objection that evolution must give any intelligence a sense of humor, then answers a different one, that ``you're not telling funny enough jokes,'' by comparison with shouting English abroad. The first objection, about minds that evolution produces, gets no answer here.}
\cpara{Says laughter can be valuable even if not all possible minds share it. The reasons are left to the author's posts on metaethics, which come much later in the book.}

\cpara{Takes the pulp-cover example from ``Mind Projection Fallacy,'' later in the book. That post offered its account of the artists with a hedge: ``Probably the artist did not even think to ask whether an alien perceives human females as attractive.'' Here the account is stated as fact: ``It just seemed to them.''}
\cpara{Says anthropomorphism cannot be dropped by an act of will, with a joke about a slime monster.}

\cpara{Offers natural selection as a maker of complex machines that has no emotions. But the imagined objection is about ``any intelligent mind,'' and the author does not count natural selection as one. ``Thou Art Godshatter'' calls evolution ``stupid in an absolute sense,'' and ``Belief in Intelligence'' puts natural selection under ``optimization process'' because ``Intelligence'' is ``too narrow a term.'' The example shows that building complex machines does not require emotions; it does not show the same for intelligence.}
\cpara{Recalls a fight against anthropomorphic thinking in evolutionary biology, without sources. ``The Tragedy of Group Selectionism,'' earlier in the book, tells one episode of it.}
\cpara{Names writers who, in the author's view, write real aliens: Jack Vance, and Niven and Pournelle.}

\cpara{The episode is ``The Omega Glory'' (1968). In Wikipedia's summary, Spock explains the likeness by a history that ``closely paralleled that of Earth,'' and the document the villagers keep is ``a version of the American Constitution.'' The attribution to Card is hedged (``I think''); I could not find the remark.}
\cpara{Concludes that failing to imagine the alien is failing to see our own humanity as special.}
